HELICAL COMPRESSION SPRINGS 

PART II SPECIFICATION FOR COLD COILED SPRINGS 
HADE FROM CIRCULAR SECTION WIRE AND BAR 



1. Scope — Covers cold coiled compression springs made from spring wires of up to 17 mm diameter, 
1 .1 This standard is applicable to springs having the following parameters: 

a) Mean coil diameter; D^ up to 200 trim, 

b) Unloaded length; £„ up to 630 mm, 

c) Number of working coils; /, > 2, and 

d) Coil ratio; w from 4 up to 20,

3. Manufacture 

3.1 Process — The manufacturing process ts governed by degree of stressing involved, the material for 
the manufacture and intended application of the spring. Cold coiling can generally be done with wires 
up to 17 mm in diameter. For wire and bar diameters between 1 and 17 mm hot coiling process may be 
used, 

3.2 Direction of CoiJing — Helical compression springs can be coiled in left-hand or right-hand directions. 
Normally they have right-hand coiling. Springs for application in nested sets (assemblies) or where 
one spring is working inside the other, direction of coiling is alternately left and right. The outer springs 
are generally with right-hand coifing. Where the springs require left-hand coiling, the same shall be 
mentioned in the order and enquiry or appropriately in IS : 7906 (Part III) -1975 'Helical compression springs: 
Part HI Data sheet for specifications for springs made from circular section wire and bar*. 

3.3 Spring Ends — For transmitting the axial loads on the connecting body, the spring ends shall be so 
formed that for any position of the spring, the spring action is axial as far as possible This is generally 
achieved by decreasing the pitch at the runout coil The spring end is then ground so that a flat seating 
surface is obtained (see Fig. 1). Other types of spring ends are shown in Fig. 2 to 5. 





<^=H 





FIG. 2 ENDS OPEN FIG. 3 ENDS OPEN FIG 4 ENDS CLOSED FIG. 5 ENDS TAPERED BEFORE 

AND UNGROUND AND GROUND AND UNGROUND COILING, CLOSED AND GROUND 

3.3.1 If the springs can be used without end grinding, for example, for wire diameters less than 1 mm 
or for coil ratio above 15, it is preferable to do so for reasons of economy 

3.3.2 For compression springs with wire diameter less then 5 rrm, grinding of the ends is not 
recommended. 

3.3.3 For simultaneous grinding of both the ends of compression springs made of wire diameters 0-5 mm 
and above, care shall be taken to see that only those springs that allow sufficient contact pressure shall 
be so ground. It has been found that the contact pressure p is approximately given by: 

p = £* ^ 003 N/mrrT- 

3.3.4 If the grinding of spring ends is not required, the springs shall be made according to Fig. 2 or 
Fig. 4. The type of spring end required shall be specified on order and enquiry. 

3.3.5 If an outside or inside chamfer at the coil runout is required, the chamfer width shall be indicated. 
The chamfer angle shall be 45° approximately.

4. Material — Springs shall be made from any of the materials specified below 

4.1 Group 1 

4.1.1 Patented and cold drawn spring steel wires, unalloyed, Grades 1, 2, 3 and 4 to IS 4454 (Part I)- 
1975 'SteeJ wires for cold formed springs Part J Patented and cold drawn steel wires -- unalloyed (first 
revision)', 

4.1 .2 Oil hardened and tempered spring steel wire and valve spring wire, unalloyed, Grades SW and VW 
to IS: 4454 (Part II) -1975 'Steel wires for cold formed springs Part l| Oil hardened and tempered spring 
steel wire and valve spring wjre — unalloyed {first revision)' 

4.1 .3 Alloyed, Oil hardened and tempered valve spring wire and spnng steel wrre for use under moderately 
elevated temperatures. Grades IS, 2S, 1 D and 2D to IS 4454 (Part 111) -1975 'Steel wires for cold formed 
Springs: Part III Oil hardened and tempered steel wires — alloyed {ftr&t revision)' . 

4.1.4 Stainless spring steel wire, Grade 1 and 2 to IS 4454 {Part IV) -1975 'Steel wires for cold formed 
springs: Part IV Stainless spring steel wires for normal corrosion resistance (first revision)' 

4.2 Group 2 

4.2.1 Hard -drawn brass wires to IS 4076- 1 967 Hard brass wires tor spring and other special purposes' 

4.2.2 Phosphor bronze wires to IS:1385-19C8 Phosuhor bronze rods and bars sheet and strip, and 
wire (first revision)'. 

4.3 Other materials, subject to agreement between the purchaser and the manufacturer, may be used. 

5. Tolerances — All tolerances specified m th.s statvimd apply to compression springs made from materials 
specified in 4.1 For springs made from materials specified in 4.2 and other materials, the tolerances shall 
be fixed by agreement between the purchaser and the manufacturer Normal tolerances for Dm, F and L Q 
are specified in Table 1, 5.2 and 5.3 For reasons ot economy, wider toleranrss given in ADpendix A should 
be used. However, where functionally required, sprngs can also be man Lectured w<rh closer tolerances 
given in Appendix B For certain types of springs, it may be essential to adopt wider tolerances given in 
Appendix A. For such cases reference should be made to the spring manufacturer. 

B.I Tolerances 7i> on Coil Diameter for Unloaded Springs -- The tolerances shall be as g-^en m Table 1 . 
It is recommended thai where a spring is working inside a sleeve or over an arbcr or bot^ in a sleeve and 
over an arbor, the minimum diameter of the sleeve and the maximum diameter of the arbor should be specified 
to ensure proper understanding of such requirements

6, Complimentary Adjustment for Manufacturing — To enable springs to be held within specified 
limits of axial loads, the manufacturer requires complimentary adjustments during production. These shall 
be specified by the following method:

6.1 The numerical values of the quantities allowed according to manufacturer's discretion for complimentary 
adjustment shall be specified in the drawing and apply as guide values only. When these are not given 
complimentary adjustments given in 6 shall apply. 

6.2 While allowing complimentary adjustments, care should be taken to see that the maximum stress on the 
springs does not exceed the maximum allowable stress for the material. 

7. Testing 

7,1 Static Load Test — This test is carried Out in the normal direction of loading with the spring standing 
vertically, tn each case before carrying out the static test the spring shall be compressed 3 times in quick 
succession to the block fengtfi or to a length corresponding to the maximum permissible static stress values, 

whichever is more. 

7.1.1 In the case of springs which are required to be tested over or in a guide, the test procedure is to be 
agreed upon with the manufacturer. 

l.Z The theoretical characteristic curve [force-deflection diagram (frg. 3J1 of a cylindrical helical com- 
pression spring is a straight line. In practice, however, the start and finish of the spring characteristic 
show a departure from linearity. If it is intended to check the spring rate by finding the characteristic of the 
spring, this test must be carried out over the range 0*3 F^ to 0-7 F m so as to cover the linearity with certainty. 
F m here corresponds to the minimum permissible test length L m of the spring. The spring rate S* is thus: 

° c ~ M "~ &f " *!-£, ~ f % -t x

(see Fig. 9).

EXPLANATORY NOTE 

This standard is one of the series ol standards on design calculation and specif i call ons of helical 
coiled springs. Other standards in this series are
